text:
# A Timeline of Alleged Drake Reference Tracks Leaking

By: **Miki Hellerbach**

There was once a time when rappers (especially those who claim to be the best in the world) were expected to pen lyrics solely by themselves. Times have changed, and rap music—which is now more closely associated with pop—has updated the way the creative process works. It has become more common for rappers, producers, and singers to adopt a more collaborative process. No one has signaled this change more than [**Drake**](https://www.complex.com/tag/drake), the most dominant rap artist of the decade.  

Since 2011, when there [were very loud whispers](https://genius.com/a/the-weeknd-claimed-he-gave-up-almost-half-of-house-of-balloons-to-drake-for-take-care) about The Weeknd’s contributions to _Take Care_, it has been commonly known that Drake uses collaborators to help with his songs and, seemingly, his verses. (When a reference track leaks, it’s not clear if the artist is getting help with their verses or flow.)  

But on July 22, 2015, Meek Mill officially broke the dam when he [tweeted](https://www.billboard.com/music/rb-hip-hop/meek-mill-drake-feud-twitter-6640964/), “Stop comparing drake to me too…. He don’t write his own raps! That’s why he ain’t tweet my album because we found out!” Later that day, it was revealed that Atlanta rapper Quentin Miller had allegedly written Drake’s verse on Meek’s 2015 single “R.I.C.O.” Soon after, Atlanta rapper OG Maco [tweeted](https://allhiphop.com/news/quentin-miller-blames-og-maco-for-exposing-him-as-drakes-ghostwriter-maco-fires-back/) a screen grab of the credits for Drake’s latest project at the time, _If You’re Reading This It’s Too Late,_ where Miller was credited as a writer on multiple songs, including “6 Man,” “10 Bands,” and “Know Yourself.” The next day, Funkmaster Flex [premiered](https://www.bet.com/article/757sgm/funkmaster-flex-leaks-drake-s-reference-track-for-10-bands) an alleged Quentin Miller reference track for “10 Bands” on Hot 97.  

While Drake ended up dominating Meek Mill in the [short-lived rap battle](https://www.complex.com/music/a/markelibert/drakes-best-diss-songs-ranked) that followed, there would be a new question mark around Drake’s hip-hop legitimacy amongst purists. Since then, ten more alleged reference tracks have been exposed adding fuel to the initial questioning of Drake’s lyrical validity. # A Timeline of Alleged Drake Reference Tracks Leaking

By: **Miki Hellerbach**

There was once a time when rappers (especially those who claim to be the best in the world) were expected to pen lyrics solely by themselves. Times have changed, and rap music—which is now more closely associated with pop—has updated the way the creative process works. It has become more common for rappers, producers, and singers to adopt a more collaborative process. No one has signaled this change more than [**Drake**](https://www.complex.com/tag/drake), the most dominant rap artist of the decade.  

Since 2011, when there [were very loud whispers](https://genius.com/a/the-weeknd-claimed-he-gave-up-almost-half-of-house-of-balloons-to-drake-for-take-care) about The Weeknd’s contributions to _Take Care_, it has been commonly known that Drake uses collaborators to help with his songs and, seemingly, his verses. (When a reference track leaks, it’s not clear if the artist is getting help with their verses or flow.)  

But on July 22, 2015, Meek Mill officially broke the dam when he [tweeted](https://www.billboard.com/music/rb-hip-hop/meek-mill-drake-feud-twitter-6640964/), “Stop comparing drake to me too…. He don’t write his own raps! That’s why he ain’t tweet my album because we found out!” Later that day, it was revealed that Atlanta rapper Quentin Miller had allegedly written Drake’s verse on Meek’s 2015 single “R.I.C.O.” Soon after, Atlanta rapper OG Maco [tweeted](https://allhiphop.com/news/quentin-miller-blames-og-maco-for-exposing-him-as-drakes-ghostwriter-maco-fires-back/) a screen grab of the credits for Drake’s latest project at the time, _If You’re Reading This It’s Too Late,_ where Miller was credited as a writer on multiple songs, including “6 Man,” “10 Bands,” and “Know Yourself.” The next day, Funkmaster Flex [premiered](https://www.bet.com/article/757sgm/funkmaster-flex-leaks-drake-s-reference-track-for-10-bands) an alleged Quentin Miller reference track for “10 Bands” on Hot 97.  

While Drake ended up dominating Meek Mill in the [short-lived rap battle](https://www.complex.com/music/a/markelibert/drakes-best-diss-songs-ranked) that followed, there would be a new question mark around Drake’s hip-hop legitimacy amongst purists. Since then, ten more alleged reference tracks have been exposed adding fuel to the initial questioning of Drake’s lyrical validity. Seeing a credit is one thing, but actually hearing another person lay down seemingly original lyrics for Drake to copy has some fans [question](https://x.com/rapdose/status/1795269488012923244?s=46&t=EOOlmb1qxLVCRu3o4tBezw)ing how much they can trust Drake’s pen at all.  

In response to all the recent leaks (there have been four this year thus far and two in the last week), we have decided to track the history of all of Drake’s alleged leaked reference tracks.

# Drake Teaches How To Write A Melody In 3 Steps

[

![How To Rap](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*kfjzjuFD_rbt-pfhVff5ew.jpeg)



](/@HowToRap?source=post_page---byline--7fb12d2f427c---------------------------------------)

9 min read

Jan 2, 2023

\--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

> A lot of artists don’t even know when they sound wrong, or off. That sounds the same as that hit that I have on the radio and it’s like, if you can’t place, if you don’t know when something’s wrong, you’re not gonna be one of the greats. You might be cool for a minute, but y’know, yeah… [— Drake on MTV, 10:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8rY3eqPJjI8&t=651s)

In this short clip from an interview with Drake in 2010, the young superstar-in-waiting outlined a facet of the philosophy that’s made him into an unrivaled, chart-topping phenom, not to mention hip-hop’s reigning king of choruses:

## 1\. Be Your Own Worst Critic

Cited by pundits and commentators as the man who took the previously entrenched boundaries between singing and rapping and co-mingled them within the mainstream space, **Drake**’s hook-laden approach to song-craft has meant that while he may not receive his proper reverence as an MC, his capacity for hit-making is undeniable.

But to be honest, the man who can now self-assuredly flex about having **_“more slaps than The Beatles”_** didn’t acquire his status as one of the all-time Billboard mainstays by spitting complex 16’s, he did so through his knack for anchoring his songs around innately catchy choruses.

Seen as one of the core elements of commercial rap as we know it today, these immediately ear-grabbing refrains are something that **Drake** can deliver at what seems like the drop of a hat.

But, as his comments here would suggest, the reason that they’ve so regularly been translated into globe-spanning mega-hits is because **Drizzy** is always looking to bring the potential of his hooks to the fore.

As opposed to weighing it up and accepting a middling effort as a placeholder, the OVO leader will discard anything which, to him, simply doesn’t reach his own unimpeachably high standards.

And if his comments to MTV are anything to go by, it’s due to the fact that he has the foresight to not see the song in a vacuum, but think about how that chorus, when properly rendered, could contribute to his legacy.

Now, if you yourself are a rapper who wants to learn how to create a legacy and learn the hidden catchy song structures of rappers like Drake, Kendrick Lamar, and J. Cole in a song-by-song training of their work, click HERE to get our 4-hour songwriting masterclass as a free bonus on that page.

However, when it comes to Drake, ashe made clear to **Elliott Wilson**, another thing that keep his hits feeling vital is that he is never looking to so much as invoke the spirit of the past when it comes to crafting a new hit.

> “I don’t wanna sound like No New Friends, I don’t wanna sound like I’m On One. I did that already- Drake on CRWN, [18:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L7BCxCjxtgg&t=730s)

## 2\. Know What Works For You

> “It shouldn’t be your tagline, I don’t even write. Yeah, we can tell, if it’s not a quality product, who cares? Maybe if you took the time to write, your s\*\*t would be a little better. Sometimes, I feel like people almost pride themselves on that and kinda look at me funny when I start writing.
> 
> It’s an individual creative process, there’s no standard. As soon as you understand that and get comfortable with yourself. I’ll pull out my phone and do that in front of everybody. It’s just about quality man and taking pride in yourself- Drake on MTV- [9:00-](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8rY3eqPJjI8&t=541s)

A viewpoint that **Drake** revealed during a discussion about **Hov** and his mentor **Lil’ Wayne**’s ability to spit off the dome at a moment’s notice, **Drizzy**’s comments speak to another tenet of his artistry that’s made him into a hit factory and that’s simply knowing what works for him.

Rather than attempting to emulate his heroes, **Drake** is a man that will studiously pour over his lyrics and hooks, optimizing them for the world long before they ever see the light of day.

By taking the time to make alterations and draw from a backlog of thoughts and vocal lines that he’s compiled, **Drizzy** can find the perfect chorus for whatever pocket he’s presented in a track.

While at the same time, remaining mindful of what it is that makes his songs tick above all else.

During an interview with **Q in Canada**, **Drizzy** explained how he may have certain tendencies when it comes to writing hooks and melodies that he uses as a rule of thumb, but they’ aren’t etched in stone.

As for him, what truly matters is that whatever he’s delivering has a deep resonance with an audience that’ll allow them to foster personal bonds to his work.

> “I do shy away from major, like major chords, major chord progressions. Those are the classic pop, those aren’t the melodies that hit you in your heart. For me, it’s minor. 40 produces in minor and I’ll find the melodies to slip around it. Is anything too sugary? It just has to have emotion behind it. Hold On, We’re Going Home, that i sa major son, but there’s emotion there.There’s points where you feel something and that’s all that matters to me, that it penetrates- [Drake on Q, 6 mins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jp_yMsBHRzY)

Striving to intercept the feelings as opposed to operating on the cerebral level that traditionally-minded MC’s would, **Drizzy**’s choruses are designed to be bellowed back at him in stadiums around the world.

Confident in straddling the line between singing and spitting bars whenever the moment calls for it, another aspect of **Drizzy**’s personalized philosophy that should be taken into account by anyone that’s looking to organically increase the commercial value of their work is that you should never shy away from making what you want to hear.

As even if you initially receive flak for your melding of styles, there’s a good chance that if you want to hear it, then someone else will feel that exact same gravitational pull towards it.

> I’ll be honest, there’s times where I feel like I like R&B music better than I like rap music. It’s just sometimes I like listening to it, whether it be classic, whether it be new. It’s just when I find myself having free time, you know, I like melody. And it’s so funny that people scrutinize me so much for melody because then another rapper will go and drop their single and the whole single is melody-driven and that’s okay because he’s allowed to do that and I’m not allowed to do that. It’s just like this crazy double standard that people have for me. — Drake on CRWN[. 21 mins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L7BCxCjxtgg&t=380s)

Although **Drake** doesn’t allow the doubts or reservations of naysayers to infringe upon his creative process, his comments to Wilson do stand in contradiction to an important side note that has stood **Drizzy** in good stead during his career.

Although he has an intrinsic feel for what makes him tick as a musician and songwriter, **Drake** is a man that understands how invaluable the input of others can be. Meaning that, ghostwriting accusations aside, Drizzy has always been willing to take the opinions of his tight-knit inner circle

From taking **Rich Paul’**s advice about making **_“Best I Ever Had”_** the first single on **_So Far Gone_** as opposed to his own personal choice of **_“Uptown”_** through to enlisting the likes of **Majid Jordan** to help him craft his biggest pop hits, **Drake** isn’t afraid to defer to the expertise or instincts of others when needed.

While in the case of his relationship with his manager, **Oliver El-Khatib**, **Drake** uses his eclectic taste in order to provide himself with new vantage points from which to attack a hook or a melody.

> When it comes to the music, he provides me with the inspiration that I need to keep pushing forward. He gives me playlists of music that I just don’t have time to go find.
> 
> He’s such an incredible mind and ear that he gives me music that no-one else listens to, so that music combined with the extreme hood shit that I listen to like LIl Herb and all this… I balance it all o[ut- Drake on CRWN, 16 mins,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zv0S7zMzAJA&t=1201s)

Like him or loathe him, **Drake** has proven himself to be a sponge for music. By soaking up as much of it as he can and harnessing the wisdom of those around him, the Toronto native has proven himself to be better equipped to make hits than practically anyone in the game. But as far as he sees it, a lot of it comes down to knowing when you’ve got magic on your hands and refusing to over analyze it into oblivion.

## 3\. Don’t Overthink It

_“God’s Plan was a song that I recorded on a whim in my condo and thought nothing of it. I only had the first verse and the hook and it leaked. People forced my hand because they were like yo, that s\*\*t sounds hard. We had to rush and turn it around because I was worried that another artist was gonna get the version and just start laying like random verses on it.I never could’ve told you a week before that God’s Plan was my single and it was going to be the biggest song of my career. A lot of this is organic, it’s not that calculated_**_.”_**[**_\- Drake_**](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/IefBTIh9tTM)

Over the course of his career, **Drake** has done it all.

Capable of making “all the player’s anthems for the real brothers” as he did on **_“Keep The Family Close”_** while also delivering tracks which are tailormade for female audiences to fervently sing back at him such as **_“God’s Plan”_** and **_“Best I Ever Had”_**, Drizzy can strike a chord with both his words and melodies like few others.

But as far as he’s concerned, there is an instinctual element to writing his biggest hits which would suggest that at times, not overthinking it is the approach that can yield the greatest success.

Adept at delivering music which is felt in the hearts of audiences on a global scale, some of **Drizzy**’s most enduring hooks have come about through the most seemingly inconspicuous of circumstances. As seen with **_“God’s Plan”_**, **Drake** heeded the warning signs that he had lightning in a bottle and struck as soon as he could. Deemed to be a motivational track that’s on about 60% of the world’s workout playlists, **Drizzy** rolled with the punches and, realizing that time was of the essence, didn’t have a window to ponder whether the song was the greatest representation of his artistry.

He simply released it to the world and let it do its thing. What’s more, it’s not even the only time that he followed his intuition– and a big, naturally occurring chorus– all the way to acclaim.

> “A lot of my hit songs I’ve written in a very short period of time. “‘Hold On, We’re Going Home,’ I felt like we finished that in like two hours…I’m not a guy that does 40 songs for a project and picks 13 of them. If I’m gonna go as far as to track over a beat I usually have the utmost faith in it that it’ll end up somewhere. I don’t really dispose of too many songs. I have stuff that didn’t make this album. But I don’t have 20 or 30 of them. I have four or five records that just didn’t make it because again I was trying to keep it concise**– Drake on Q,** [**4:02-**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jp_yMsBHRzY)

Never one to opt for the **Migos** approach of laying down as many tracks as he can conceivably can and sifting through them, **Drake** is laser focused on crafting hits and it’s a lesson that anyone who’s looking to produce music with an enduring appeal should aim to emulate.

Much like **Drake**, those who seek to fuse moments of musical euphoria into their sound won’t ever reach their potential if they’re only aiming for trends. As when you consider that **_“Hold On, We’re Going Home”_** came about in unassuming fashion and has gone on to become a track for the ages, it reminds us all why we, like **Drake**, should always aim to hit upon something pure and honest. As if there’s anything that will never, ever go out of style, it’s tracks that touch to the inner-depths of the soul.

_“In approaching this album I was like man, it would be great if we had a record that was played at weddings in 10 years or that people that are away from their families in the army could listen to”_, **Drake** said in an interview with MTV shortly before the release of **_Nothing Was The Same_**_. “Something that just \[has\] timeless writing, timeless melody.”_

Through **Drizzy**’s record-setting example, the keys to writing legendary, generation-defining tracks are not only laid bare, but shown to be remarkably simplistic and obtainable.

An artist who holds fast to a sense of what makes his songs tick, **Drizzy**’s adaptable approach means that whether you have to scrap everything you’ve done in order to recalibrate or if the song practically falls into your lap in a mere matter of hours, all that really matters is that it has the capacity to stir emotion in the listener.

As if it does, then there’s no telling how far it could take you and your career.

# Studio Sessions | Boi-1da talks making hits with Drake, NFTs, and his upcoming album

There’s a good chance [if you look at the credits](/news/2021/10/28/22751118/drake-thinks-eminem-is-underappreciated) of the biggest songs of [Drake’s career](/news/2021/10/28/22751118/drake-thinks-eminem-is-underappreciated), Boi-1da’s name will be there. The multi-platinum producer has been by the rapper’s side for more than 15 years and knows what sacrifices have to be made to make classics.

“That night, I think all my friends were going out while I was working on ‘God’s Plan.’ I was [adding a drum track to it](/studio-sessions) and some bass. I was contemplating going out but I fought myself to stay in the studio,” Boi-1da [told REVOLT](/interviews).

In this installment of “Studio Sessions,” [the Grammy award-winning](/new-music/2021/1/29/22256440/meek-mill-leslie-grace-boi-1da-conga-song) producer explains how he and Drake make their hits, how NFTs are starting a producer revolution, and unreleased [music](/new-music) he hopes comes out one day. Read the chat below!

**What was the first studio session where you felt like you made it?**

The first one was when I ended up going [into the studio](/studio-sessions) with Saukrates, a legendary Canadian artist, and Kardinal Official. Kardinal was the first rapper to [make it out of Toronto](/news/2021/10/28/22751118/drake-thinks-eminem-is-underappreciated) onto the American mainstream. I was probably 17 when I was first in the studio with Kardinal. I think Drake and I were in there. This was probably in 2007.

**You produced a few records for Kardinal Official around that time. Did those come from that first session?**

[That first session](/studio-sessions) was before I worked with him. I don’t think I got to play anything. It was more of a meet-up thing. Afterward, we linked up. I remember him saying on a podcast I used to come over to his house using this busted Acer laptop, and played him all those records he ended up taking for [his album](/new-music) like “Set It Off,” “Gimme Some,” and “Lighters.”

**Who was the first artist you really collaborated with in the studio?**

The first artist I was really working with [was definitely Drake](/news/2021/10/28/22751118/drake-thinks-eminem-is-underappreciated). We met when we were 17. I remember the first day I met him. We made one of the dopest records we ever made at the time. We made this record called “Do What You Do.” He was the first artist I felt I had chemistry with.

**What is a typical session with you and Drake like? I’m assuming 40 is there.**

40 is there sometimes. Usually, 40 and [Drake](/news/2021/10/28/22751118/drake-thinks-eminem-is-underappreciated) will do their thing and I’ll pull up on them. With me, I may pull up stuff and Drake will pick something or he’ll have something he wants me to work on. I may also [just vibe out and play some beats](/studio-sessions). The process is different every time. We don’t have a lot of footage of us in the studio because I don’t really pull out phones and cameras in the studio a lot. We just get to it. There’s no-nonsense in there.

**What’s a noticeable suggestion you’ve made on a Drake record?**

I’ll do that with other artists, but I have so much trust in Drake, I don’t suggest anything to him because he knows what to do already. [He has a long-standing record](/new-music) of killing everything, so when it comes to a guy like that, you just give him what he needs and it’s over from there. He’s a machine.

**Next month is the 10-year anniversary of _Take Care_. You produced “Headlines.” Are there any _Take Care_\-era songs you did that never came out?**

Yeah. Around that time, [we had a lot of records](/new-music) we were doing together. I did the first single, but in the same year, I was having a kid and I had a lot going on. I wasn’t there a lot, which is why I only [have one song on the album](/new-music). I ended up doing a very important song. Life has to sometimes slow you down for a bit. I was taking care of my child for the most part. [For the next album](/new-music), I was very present and all over it.

**You tweeted recently that you’re working on your own project. What’s going on with that?**

I’m working on [a series of compilation albums](/new-music) with some of your favorite artists. That’s the most information I can give you. It’s going to be really dope. There’ll be a lot of collabs, cool ideas, and dope beats. I’ve been working on it slowly, but I’m about to go full drive into it.

**Are there older songs that’ll be on these compilations?**

I got some stuff from a year ago that is going to make it on there. But, I just want to perfect everything and then put it out. [It’s going to have collabs](/new-music) you wouldn’t expect.

**You’re also helping the next generation of producers as part of Bacardi’s** **[Music Liberates Music program](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eFZjVvI5hcQ)** **by helping them create an NFT mixtape. Did you work hands-on with the producers?**

[The whole purpose of this mixtape](/new-music) is to shine a light on female producers in the industry. A lot of times, female producers get overshadowed. This movement Bacardi has started means a lot to me. I just coached them and listened to what they were doing to give them feedback. I didn’t directly produce anything. The music from [all three of the producers](/studio-sessions) — Bambii, Denise De’ion, and PERFXN — are from really dope producers. I sat with them and just listened to the music. The NFTs also allow fans to become part of the music and share royalties with the producers. That’s dope.

**NFTs allow the creator to continuously get paid for their work. When it comes to that, how revolutionary is that for producers?**

This is very revolutionary for producers. I’m thankful Bacardi put this together because it [changes the game for producers](/studio-sessions). We’re always in the background, so we don’t always get that much visibility. NFTs are changing the narrative.

   ![](./media_12351cb47d92886c31bfadb1656b9b54964566568.jpg?width=750&format=jpg&optimize=medium)

Denise De’ion(left), Boi1da (center), Bambii (near right), PERFXN (far right)

Bacardi Rum

**What do you need in the studio to make your best music?**

All I need are [some good speakers](/studio-sessions) and sub-woofers. There can be anything going on in the studio and I won’t pay attention. I’m laser-focused. Funny story, I remember going to the studio for the first time with 40 when I was still using that old broken computer I made “Best I Ever Had,” “Forever,” “Not Afraid” and [so many other hit records on](/studio-sessions). First time I went in the studio with 40, I plugged my computer in and he told me, “Yo, your computer is making a buzzing sound. You don’t hear it?” I actually didn’t hear it until he showed me. That’s how focused I am with the music.

**What’s the most star-studded session you were in?**

[I was in the studio once](/studio-sessions) with Timbaland, Drake, and [Puff Daddy](/sean-diddy-combs) at the same time. That was a crazy session. I’ve also been in the studio with Dr. Dre years ago. I was super stoked. Dre is my idol. I was in the studio shivering because I was in the same vicinity.

**How did the pandemic affect how you made music in 2020?**

[I love to collaborate with other producers](/studio-sessions) and I wasn’t able to go to L.A. — or America in general — for a bit. In the beginning, the pandemic killed the vibe to the point I didn’t feel like making music. After a while, [I was able to travel again](/tour-tales) and go to America to see my people. I don’t like working at my house because you’re too comfortable there.

**Who was the first artist you were in the studio with?**

Other than Drake, I’ve pulled up on [A$AP Rocky](/news/2021/10/24/22743577/asap-rockys-live-love-asap-will-be-re-released-on-streaming-platforms). We did some cool stuff.

**You said before that “God’s Plan” was made the same night you made “Diplomatic Immunity.” What was happening in that session?**

I think I was at Nightbird Studios L.A. [That studio has some magic in there](/studio-sessions). That night, I think all my friends were going out while I was working on “God’s Plan.” I was adding a drum track to it and some bass. I was contemplating going out, but I fought myself to stay in the studio. I got those two off and I got up out of there.

**How did you end up on Kanye West’s “Ok, Ok”?**

That was an idea I did with Vory a little bit ago. [Kanye](/news/2021/9/14/22674562/styles-p-drake-kanye-west-feud-worthless-battle) and Vory elaborated on it a little more and finished the song. I’ve been pretty mutual with Kanye. Obviously, there has been [stuff going on between Kanye and Drake](/news/2021/9/14/22674562/styles-p-drake-kanye-west-feud-worthless-battle). But, at the time they were cool and the song was done a while ago. Kanye took a bunch of stuff out of the beat. That’s why it sounds bare bones, but it still sounds good.

**What is the one unreleased song you wish would come out one day?**

[On my Verzuz battle](/news/2021/10/19/22735121/rappers-turned-down-request-to-compete-busta-rhymes-in-verzuz), I previewed a song with Drake and Roddy Ricch. It’s pretty hard. I’d love for the song to come out, but it’s out of my control.

**What’s coming up for you for the rest of the year and 2022?**

I can’t ruin any of the surprises but there’s a lot of fire. This has been a great year for me musically and creatively. I feel I’ve been making some of [the best music](/news/2021/10/19/22735121/rappers-turned-down-request-to-compete-busta-rhymes-in-verzuz) of my life this year.

**I hope one of those collaborations is with** **[Kendrick Lamar](/news/2021/10/21/22738607/fans-think-kendrick-lamar-may-release-his-new-album-soon)** **because “Blacker The Berry” is one of my favorite beats from you.**

I can’t say much about that. But, stay tuned.

# "We started it": Drake's producer Gordo on reclaiming Black dance music on Honestly, Nevermind

The standout track from Drake's surprise album was assembled in the sky between Dallas and Toronto. Back in May, DJ Gordo had flown to Brazil to play the sunrise set at Tribe festival, and on the way home from São Paulo he started to come down with something. By the time he landed for a layover he felt even worse, but a selection of tracks which arrived from the Australian artist and songwriter Ry X – sent as inspiration for a new secret Drake album – quickly brought him back to life.

“I started sampling an MP3 record of his and chopping it up,” Gordo tells _GQ_. “I ended up making the "Sticky" beat on the plane. I texted \[Drake\], and when he replied at 4pm I was already in the kitchen at his house. I played him the beat and he was like, “Woah”. At that moment J. Cole walked in because he was at the house playing basketball. They recorded that night."

DJ Gordo – formerly known as Carnage, and whose passport reads Diamanté Anthony Blackmon – has been close friends with Drake for years, his own music career leading him to collaborate with artists including [A$AP Rocky](https://www.gq-magazine.co.uk/gallery/asap-rocky-best-outfits), [Lil Uzi Vert](https://www.gq.com/story/lil-uzi-vert-fit-pic-profile) and Migos. On _Honestly, Nevermind,_ the record which landed as a surprise in the early hours of Friday morning, and which represents a seismic shift towards dance music for the rapper, Gordo has been hugely influential by producing six of the 14 tracks.

The album is an homage to the Baltimore club music that Gordo remembers hearing in his auntie and mum's cars, playing out on the radio stations of Maryland: tracks from the likes of DJ K-Swift and Quicksilva, which shudder against a slowly pulsing beat and kick pattern. The “vibey” kind of house music on _Honestly, Nevermind_ was also influenced by electronic artists like the Keine Music artists &Me, Adam Port and Rampa.

But for Gordo, Black artists turning to club music is less of a departure and more of a return. “There’s always been this weird thing in the dance world where the majority of DJs are white," he says. "But we all know that house music back in the day in Chicago and Detroit comes from the Black community and gay community. We started it, and now, you know, all the biggest stars and DJs in the entire world, the majority of them, are white.”

_Honestly, Nevermind,_ then, can be read as more political than just a summer dance-floor moment for Drake. The kind of house music which it riffs on is often heard in the rarified spaces of Ibiza and Mykonos: the sleek and sexy music of the ultra-wealthy which often sanitises the Black roots of house music. It's an album that wants you to have a good time, but make no mistake: it's also an act of reclamation.

# "We started it": Drake's producer Gordo on reclaiming Black dance music on Honestly, Nevermind

The standout track from Drake's surprise album was assembled in the sky between Dallas and Toronto. Back in May, DJ Gordo had flown to Brazil to play the sunrise set at Tribe festival, and on the way home from São Paulo he started to come down with something. By the time he landed for a layover he felt even worse, but a selection of tracks which arrived from the Australian artist and songwriter Ry X – sent as inspiration for a new secret Drake album – quickly brought him back to life.

“I started sampling an MP3 record of his and chopping it up,” Gordo tells _GQ_. “I ended up making the "Sticky" beat on the plane. I texted \[Drake\], and when he replied at 4pm I was already in the kitchen at his house. I played him the beat and he was like, “Woah”. At that moment J. Cole walked in because he was at the house playing basketball. They recorded that night."

DJ Gordo – formerly known as Carnage, and whose passport reads Diamanté Anthony Blackmon – has been close friends with Drake for years, his own music career leading him to collaborate with artists including [A$AP Rocky](https://www.gq-magazine.co.uk/gallery/asap-rocky-best-outfits), [Lil Uzi Vert](https://www.gq.com/story/lil-uzi-vert-fit-pic-profile) and Migos. On _Honestly, Nevermind,_ the record which landed as a surprise in the early hours of Friday morning, and which represents a seismic shift towards dance music for the rapper, Gordo has been hugely influential by producing six of the 14 tracks.

The album is an homage to the Baltimore club music that Gordo remembers hearing in his auntie and mum's cars, playing out on the radio stations of Maryland: tracks from the likes of DJ K-Swift and Quicksilva, which shudder against a slowly pulsing beat and kick pattern. The “vibey” kind of house music on _Honestly, Nevermind_ was also influenced by electronic artists like the Keine Music artists &Me, Adam Port and Rampa.

But for Gordo, Black artists turning to club music is less of a departure and more of a return. “There’s always been this weird thing in the dance world where the majority of DJs are white," he says. "But we all know that house music back in the day in Chicago and Detroit comes from the Black community and gay community. We started it, and now, you know, all the biggest stars and DJs in the entire world, the majority of them, are white.”

_Honestly, Nevermind,_ then, can be read as more political than just a summer dance-floor moment for Drake. The kind of house music which it riffs on is often heard in the rarified spaces of Ibiza and Mykonos: the sleek and sexy music of the ultra-wealthy which often sanitises the Black roots of house music. # Here Are All the Hot 100 Records That Drake Has (and Hasn’t) Broken

Every new [Drake](https://www.billboard.com/artist/drake) release seems to bring another piece of _Billboard_ chart history.

Since first appearing on the [Billboard Hot 100](https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100/) dated May 23, 2009, with his breakthrough hit “Best I Ever Had” (which peaked at No. 2), Drake has shattered record after record and reached unprecedented chart heights.

* * *

In 2015, he became just the fourth artist in history to earn 100 career Hot 100 entries. He joined the 200-hit club in 2019, then became the first (and still only) artist to reach 300 entries in 2023. In 2026, he extended that record even further, becoming the only artist ever to amass 400 career Hot 100 entries.

Among Drake’s many other Hot 100 achievements are the records for the most top two, top three, top five, top 10, top 20 and top 40 hits, along with the most No. 1 debuts in the chart’s history.

He also holds the record for the most No. 1 Hot 100 hits among solo male artists, with 14. Among all artists, he’s tied with Rihanna and Taylor Swift for the third-most No. 1s overall, after only the Beatles (20) and Mariah Carey (19).

As Drake continues adding to his resume, here’s a look at every major Hot 100 record the superstar has broken throughout his career — and the milestones he hasn’t reached (yet) — through the chart dated May 30, 2026.

_It’s also worth noting that the rise of streaming has drastically reshaped how artists accumulate Hot 100 records. In recent years, blockbuster album releases have allowed acts to chart multiple songs simultaneously, a stark contrast to earlier eras when artists typically promoted one radio single at a time in a largely physical-sales-driven marketplace. That shift in consumption helps explain why modern artists have been able to rapidly increase their career totals for Hot 100 entries and other chart milestones._

## Most Top Two Hot 100 Hits

Drake has tallied 27 songs that have peaked in the top two on the Hot 100. That’s the most among all artists in chart history.

## Most Top Three Hot 100 Hits

Drake has charted a record 35 songs that have peaked in the top three.

## Most Top Five Hot 100 Hits

Drake has earned a record 47 top five hits on the Hot 100.

## Most Top 10 Hot 100 Hits

Drake has tallied a record 90 top 10 hits on the Hot 100.

## Most Top 20 Hot 100 Hits

Drake has tallied a record 154 top 20 hits on the Hot 100.

## Most Top 40 Hot 100 Hits

Drake has accumulated a record 241 top 40 hits on the Hot 100.

## Most Total Hot 100 Hits

Drake has charted a record 402 career songs on the Hot 100, the most by any artist in the chart’s history. He has also appeared on three additional charting songs for which he did not receive official credit, meaning they do not count toward his career total: Young Money’s “Every Girl” (No. 10 peak in 2009), Young Money’s “Bedrock” (No. 2, 2010), and Travis Scott’s “Sicko Mode” (No. 1, 2018).

Drake reached his 100th career Hot 100 entry in 2015 following the release of his collaborative album with Future, _What a Time to Be Alive_, and earned his 200th entry in 2019 after dropping _Care Package_. He later became the first artist to reach 300 career Hot 100 entries with _For All the Dogs_ in 2023, and the first to hit the 400-song milestone in 2026 following the simultaneous release of _ICEMAN_, _HABIBTI_ and _MAID OF HONOUR_.

## Most No. 2-Peaking Hot 100 Hits

Drake has earned the most songs that have peaked at No. 2 on the Hot 100, with 13.

## Most No. 1 Hot 100 Debuts

Drake has a record 10 No. 1 debuts on the Hot 100: “God’s Plan,” “Nice for What,” “Toosie Slide,” “What’s Next,” “Way 2 Sexy” (featuring Future & Young Thug), “Wait For U” (with Future & Tems), “Jimmy Cooks” (featuring 21 Savage), “Slime You Out” (featuring SZA), “First Person Shooter” (featuring J. Cole) and “Janice STFU.”

## Most Top Five Hot 100 Debuts

Drake has a record 36 songs that have debuted in the top five of the Hot 100.

## Most Top 10 Hot 100 Debuts

Drake has a record 74 songs that have debuted in the top 10 of the Hot 100.

## Most Top 20 Hot 100 Debuts

Drake has a record 130 songs that have debuted in the top 20 of the Hot 100.

## Most Top 40 Hot 100 Debuts

Drake has a record 207 songs that have debuted in the top 40 of the Hot 100.

## Most Consecutive Weeks Spent on the Hot 100

Drake spent a record 431 consecutive weeks on the Hot 100, from May 23, 2009, through Aug. 19, 2017.

## Most Songs in the Top Five Simultaneously (shared record)

Drake, The Beatles, Taylor Swift and Kendrick Lamar are the only artists in history to occupy the entire top five of the Hot 100 in a single week. As a result, they share the record for the most concurrent top five hits in a single week.

The Beatles became the first act to achieve the feat on April 4, 1964, followed by Drake on Sept. 18, 2021; Swift on Nov. 5, 2022, and again on May 4, 2024, and Oct. 18, 2025; and Lamar on Dec. 7, 2024.

## Most Songs in the Top 20 Simultaneously (shared record)

Drake set the record for the most concurrent top 20 hits in a single week when he placed 15 songs in the region on the Nov. 19, 2022-dated Hot 100 following the release of _Her Loss_ with 21 Savage. He achieved the feat again on May 30, 2026, when he charted 15 songs in the region from _ICEMAN_

Taylor Swift later matched the feat on the May 4, 2024-dated chart, when she simultaneously charted 15 top 20 hits from _The Tortured Poets Department_.

## Most Songs on the Hot 100 Simultaneously

Drake charted a record 42 songs on the Hot 100 simultaneously on May 30, 2026, thanks to tracks from _ICEMAN, HABIBTI_ and _MAID OF HONOUR._ That’s the most entries on the chart in a single week.

## Most Weeks Spent at No. 1 in a Calendar Year

Drake spent 29 weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 in 2018, thanks to “God’s Plan” (11 weeks), “Nice For What” (eight weeks) and “In My Feelings” (10 weeks). That’s the most weeks spent on top in a single calendar year.

## Most Top 10 Hits Earned in a Calendar Year

Drake earned 13 top 10 hits on the Hot 100 in 2018, 2021 and 2022. That’s the most ever in a single year.

## Most Cumulative Weeks Spent in the Top 10

Drake has spent 412 total weeks in the top 10 of the Hot 100 in his career (combining the totals of all his 90 top 10s), the most of all time.

## Most Positions Peaked At on the Hot 100

Drake has peaked at, astonishingly, 95 of the Hot 100’s 100 ranks. The only spots at which songs of his haven’t peaked: Nos. 46, 77, 96, 98 and 99.

## Hasn’t Broken

And now for some of the Hot 100 records Drake hasn’t broken (yet):

**Most No. 1 Hits**  
Drake has earned 14, while the Beatles hold the all-time record with 20.

**Most Cumulative Weeks Spent at No. 1**  
Drake has spent 57 total weeks at No. 1, while Mariah Carey holds the all-time record, with 101 weeks.

**Most Songs in the Top 10 Simultaneously  
**Taylor Swift has claimed the entire top 10 on three occasions. Drake’s personal best is nine songs in the top 10 on both Sept. 18, 2021, and May 30, 2026.

**Most Songs in the Top 40 Simultaneously**  
Taylor Swift holds the record for the most songs in the top 40 simultaneously, with 26 on May 4, 2024. Drake’s personal best is 24 on May 30, 2026.

**Most No. 1 Hits Earned in a Calendar Year**  
The Beatles hold the record for the most No. 1s earned in a calendar year, with six in 1964. Drake’s personal best is three in 2018.

**Most Top Five Hits Earned in a Calendar Year**  
The Beatles hold the record for the most top five hits earned in a calendar year, with 10 in 1964. Drake’s personal best is eight in 2021 and 2023.

**Most Top 40 Hits Earned in a Calendar Year**  
Taylor Swift holds the record for the most top 40 hits earned in a calendar year, with 40 in 2023. Drake’s personal best is 32 in 2023.

**Most Overall Hot 100 Hits Earned in a Calendar Year**  
The _Glee_ cast holds the record for the most charted songs in a calendar year, with 80 in 2010. Drake’s personal best is 40 in 2022. Taylor Swift holds the record for the most by a traditional artist, with 54 in 2023.

**Song With the Most Weeks Spent at No. 1**  
Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas is You” is the longest-leading No. 1 hit of all time, with 22 weeks on top. Drake’s longest-leading No. 1 hit is “God’s Plan” at 11 weeks.

**Song With the Most Weeks Spent in the Top Five**  
Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” has spent the most weeks in the top five (47 weeks). Drake’s song with the most weeks spent in the top five is “God’s Plan” (22).

**Song With the Most Weeks Spent in the Top 10**  
Teddy Swims’ “Lose Control” has spent the most weeks in the top 10 (80 weeks). Drake’s song with the most weeks spent in the top 10 is “God’s Plan” (26).

**Song With the Most Weeks Spent in the Top 20**  
Teddy Swims’ “Lose Control” has spent the most weeks in the top 20 (90 weeks). Drake’s song with the most weeks spent in the top 20 is “No Guidance” (Chris Brown featuring Drake) (31).

**Song With the Most Weeks Spent in the Top 40**  
Teddy Swims’ “Lose Control” has spent the most weeks in the top 20 (94 weeks). Drake’s song with the most weeks spent in the top 40 is “No Guidance” (Chris Brown featuring Drake) (44).

**Song With the Most Weeks Spent on the Hot 100**  
Teddy Swims’ “Lose Control” has spent the most weeks on the Hot 100 (112 weeks). Drake’s longest-charting song is “No Guidance” (Chris Brown featuring Drake) (46).

Around the time Drake announced he was working on a new album, GORDO—Drake’s close friend of over 12 years and one of the producer’s on _Honestly, Nevermind_—was touring the world, making stops at major festivals like Coachella and Lollapalooza as a DJ. They would talk via phone when they had a chance, but with their busy schedules, they weren’t able to lock in on music at the time. Then, a couple months ago, GORDO got a request from Drake: “send me some stuff.”

That’s how GORDO landed production credits on two tracks off Drake’s newly released album. The producer, whose credits on the album include “Gently” featuring Bad Bunny and “Rich Baby Daddy” with SZA and Sexyy Red, reveals Drake was on a mission to find something unique for his new project. “He told me that he needed something different,” he tells Complex. “Weeks and weeks and weeks… we sat there for a long time trying to figure out what I \[could\] bring to the table.”

Over the last year, GORDO has worked on hit Latin records like Maluma’s “Parcera” and “Hombres y Mujeres” with Feid. He is also still on a high from the release when we chat over Zoom, but when asked about what’s next, he quotes a text message from Drake: “your album is next.” “\[It’s coming\] very, very soon,” the producer continues. “You already know how diverse I am, imagine my fucking album. And I have one of the greatest to ever do it on my side.”

While we keep our eyes peeled for the producer’s forthcoming album, check out Drake’s _For All The Dogs,_ and Complex’s interview with GORDO below.

**Around the beginning of the pandemic you changed your name from Carnage to GORDO. How have you grown into that persona in the last few years?**  
Instead of growing into GORDO, I think I shrunk into GORDO. Before the pandemic, I was really unhealthy. I was almost 400 pounds. I was really overweight. I was really sick. I had a complete lifestyle change, musically, mentally, spiritually, everything. I mean, it's really been night and day, you know. People make a big deal about losing 15 or 20 pounds. Imagine losing a grown man. Yeah, it's been a completely new outlook on life.

**What do you think is the biggest defining trait of GORDO as an artist?**  
I used to characterize Carnage as obnoxious and loud. So the opposite of that would be emotional, caring, loving, sexy, maturity… I've matured. I think out of all those keywords, maturity is my favorite. I've grown sonically. It used to just be about how loud and how quick and how fast I can get you from zero to 100. Now it's about making love. I like taking my time with things and enjoying the process.

**I understand you and Drake have been friends for quite some time now, but how did you first link up?**  
Twelve years ago we met on Christian Mingle, and you know, he swiped up and we linked up. He liked my profile and liked his and we just hit it off… We met up once at a communion and it went great. _\[Laughs.\]_

I met this guy so long ago through one of my homies. It was like a Lil Wayne show. There's a photo out there somewhere of when we first met him. We've always had a lot of mutual friends. So we always stayed connected here and there. And then in 2017 \[or\] 2016, we started getting closer and closer. Then there was a long time that we didn't talk. But as of recently, we became really close musically. We never talked about music until last year and we've been friends for years. I think that's the coolest part of it, is it was never about music. We were just homies. We have the same brain. We always say that if we were in high school, we would have been best friends.

**With _For All The Dogs_, did Drake communicate what sound he was looking for?**  
No, not at all. I didn't know he was working on an album. Actually, he's always working on music. But it wasn't like a thing where we sat down and he was like, “this is what we're gonna do.” I hadn't seen him this entire year that he's been working. I've been touring. That's the thing, all his boys and all the homies that produce for him are always around him all the time. I'm kind of like the only one touring every day so I don't see him that much. I haven't been around, so I've been really out of the loop with this album. But he's always like, “send me some stuff,” and I always send him stuff. But a couple of months ago, he told me that he needed something different. Weeks and weeks and weeks, we were trying to find something different. And if you listen to “Rich Baby Daddy,” that's the only record on that album that's like that. It brings out the Miami bass vibe, that two-step vibe that you haven't heard from any artist in a long time. We sat there for a long time trying to figure out what I \[could\] bring to the table.

**What was the process like of trying to find something different?**  
The process is sending him stuff and him not saying anything and then sending him stuff and him being like, “oh my God, this is it.” That's literally the process. And then it's like, “maybe, try a different sample.” Then it's me hitting up all my homies and shit trying to see what homies have a new vibe and a new sound so I could touch that up and try to flip that into something.

**How did “Gently” with Bad Bunny come together?**  
That was a record that OZ and Drake had started a while back. I was really out of the loop with this cause I'm constantly doing my own shit. But obviously he doesn't speak Spanish. So, one day he's like, “yo, me and \[Bad\] Bunny did a crazy record.” I'm like, “no way!” He's like, “I'm gonna send it to you,” and he sent it to me and he's singing in Spanish and shit. He's like, “I just sent it to Bad Bunny, let's see what he does with it.” So I had heard his verse, the original first part with him, and then a couple weeks later he's like, “Bunny did his verse, I don't understand shit. So I'm gonna send it to you.” And he sent it to me because obviously Spanish is my first language. Then I listen to it and I'm like, “holy shit, this is crazy!” And he's like, “yeah, but like, we need to take it to the next level.” So I got the stems for it. The Bunny part was the part that I produced. I sent it to him and he was like, “holy fucking shit,” and then he sent it to Bad Bunny, and he was like, “holy fucking shit.”

**So, Drake recorded the first part of the song prior to you hopping on the production side of it, but have you ever given him pointers on singing in Spanish?**  
No, but he’s a big fan of me, so he definitely looks at my Instagram sometimes just to get inspiration, just looks at my face and tries to channel his inner GORDO. No, but he speaks Spanish pretty well. I've never really been around him when he's in his writing. He usually just locks himself up and does everything by himself. And in the studio he just does everything and then you just wake up and he does like five songs in one night. It's just like a fucking genius crazy.

**Latin music is becoming more and more popular and mainstream with artists like Bad Bunny. What is something you hope to see for the genre as it continues to soar?**  
I actually don't really need to see more. I think where it's at right now is great. I think when things get too big that's when shit gets oversaturated and it goes to shit. So I think it's good. I mean, it's at the top right now. Latin music can't get bigger than what it is right now.

**Some complaints from fans have been that it might already be getting oversaturated or bogged down by non-Latin artists. Do you have any thoughts about that or would you say that’s just a “fan complaint?”**  
Yeah, that's a fan thing. That happens with everything. That happens with your favorite doughnut shop down the street. You're like, “oh everyone knows that it's there and now it sucks.” It's whatever. That's people being upset that it's not their little secret anymore. That's just the way of life, everything recycles, everything goes in circles. So let's just enjoy it where it's at and then when it disappears, we'll talk about how great it was. So let's enjoy it and remember it.

**You spoke about trying to find something different and that’s how “Rich Baby Daddy” with SZA and Sexyy Red came about. But can you speak more on the process of producing that record?**  
**“**Rich Baby Daddy” was a record that I did with Johan and Richard, my homies who I work a lot with. They did “Massive,” “Calling Your Name,” and a bunch of stuff from _Honestly, Nevermind_. And when Drake had reached out and was like, let's get some more shit done for this album, Those are the guys that I always hit up. I have over 12 years of doing this, so I’ve collected such an insane group of producers and guys that are next level. So, when I was doing _Honestly, Nevermind_, I hit up all my homies to see what everyone was working on.

Back in the day when I was doing the Carnage stuff, EDM is a place where producers get the recognition they deserve. And it's funny because producers in the hip-hop world, they're respected, because it's the rapper and the beat, there are two portions of the song. But in EDM, you have the producer who produced the music and the producer is also an artist. So it’s all lights on the DJ because that's his song, so back in the day, I would try to finish everything myself. There was always a stigma of if you did this with this other guy, it's like he's a ghost producer. So for the longest time, I would produce stuff, mix and master everything myself, and obviously that would diminish how great a song is gonna be. Look at the greatest artists out there. Look at Kanye. Kanye is a producer. We all know he's a genius producer, but if you look at his songs, there's like seven or eight producers on every song because he's finding the best of the best of the best… You have to put your ego to the side. It's not all about just you doing everything. Obviously there are producers out there that do everything and we all wish we could be those guys. But Kanye, Dr. Dre and all these guys, they have no problem saying let me bring this guy over here.

So when Drake reaches out to me do I just try to do it all myself or do I fucking try to make the best music possible? With “Rich Baby Daddy,” we were trying to find this new sound. I was making a bunch of stuff, and it wasn't happening. I needed to find something. So when we were sitting there and he was like we need a new vibe, I remembered earlier that day, I had listened to \[K.P. & Envyi’s “Swing My Way”\], and I was like, no one's done that in a long time. So then I hit him and I was like, maybe we should do something like that. I reached out to Richard and Johan and we, and they made 10, 18 beats. I made a couple beats and we compiled a bunch of these bounces and I sent it to him. He was like, “this is it! But let's try different samples.” Then I went back to drawing board with Richard and Johan and we tried a couple of different things and boom, this is the fucking one.

**Gotta love the collaborative effort. Having worked on Drake’s most recent solo albums, what’s something you’ve learned about him in this era of his artistry?**  
He’s a mad man. He's insane. He doesn't sleep. He just works, works, works, works. He'll call me at 9 a.m., 10 a.m. in the morning. I'm like, bro, “go to bed. You're insane.” So that's what I learned.

**You said in a 2022 interview with [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/music-news/carnage-gordo-new-project-interview-1235070659/) that you’ve felt like an outsider even with your previous success. How are you feeling about your position or status with the release of _For All The Dogs_ today?**  
It's funny, because the record that we put out, Drake and Bad Bunny and then you have Drake, SZA, and Sexyy Red on a record and it's a hip-hop record. And if you look at my discography and all these records I put out, they're all very special and different records. I've never fit this mold. If you think of fire hip-hop producers you don't think of GORDO or Carnage. If you think of who's a fire Latin producer, you don’t think of GORDO or Carnage. If you think who's a guy that had the Soundcloud era on lit with Lil Pump and Lil Yachty and Famous Dex, or the Mac Miller songs with Cole Bennett, or Lil Uzi… If you go back and look at all those songs, you can't categorize any of those. I'm like this floating thing that's floating around from realm to realm. You can't really categorize me. So I guess that's what makes me an outsider. I'm completely OK with being an outsider and creating my own little world.

**Are titles like Best Producer Alive or Producer of the Year important to you?**  
No. No, not at all. The only title I'd be proud of would be most diverse.

**House and dance music saw a rise in popularity over the last few years thanks to projects like _Honestly, Nevermind_ and Beyonce’s _Renaissance_. Are you seeing that trend falling off or growing?**  
Dance music fell off a couple of years ago, and I think it's having a resurgence now. It's bigger than it's ever been. Music recycles itself, so everything is in the ‘90s right now. With the Weeknd, we were in the ‘80s, but I think right we're entering the ‘90s. If you really look at dance music, it's very ‘90s dance right now. And if you look at hip-hop, all the really mainstream stuff is sizzling away right now. There's a lot of more boom bap rap that's really big right now. Even internationally, look at guys like Santa Fe Klan, he’s like the biggest rapper in Mexico and selling out stadiums and he's rapping on old Ice Cube type beats like boom bap, West coast, Dr. Dre type beats. This is what kids are listening to.

**What else are you working on that you can share with us?**  
I'm gonna quote Drake right now. He [says](https://www.instagram.com/gordoszn/?img_index=1), “your album is next.” And of course, Drake is a big part of it. So it's going to be very special. \[It’s coming\] very, very soon. So, you already know how diverse I am, imagine my fucking album. And I have the one of the greatest to ever do it on my side. Now that I finished all the Drake stuff, I’m focused on GORDO now 100 percent. So, we’ll see what happens.

_**Some Sexy Songs 4 U**_ (stylized as _**$ome $exy $ongs 4 U**_ or shortened to _**$$$4U**_)[\[2\]](#cite_note-$$$-2) is a collaborative studio album by Canadian musicians [PartyNextDoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PartyNextDoor "PartyNextDoor") and [Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake_\(musician\) "Drake (musician)"). It was released on February 14, 2025, by [OVO Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OVO_Sound "OVO Sound"), Santa Anna, and [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). The album features guest appearances from [Pimmie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pimmie "Pimmie"), [Yebba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yebba "Yebba"), and [Chino Pacas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chino_Pacas "Chino Pacas"). Production on the album was handled by PartyNextDoor and Drake's frequent collaborators [Noel Cadastre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OVO_Sound "OVO Sound"), [Gordo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordo_\(DJ\) "Gordo (DJ)"), and Jordan Ullman of [Majid Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majid_Jordan "Majid Jordan"), among others.

Originally set to release in late-2024, _Some Sexy Songs 4 U_ was delayed several times. The album serves as a follow-up to the artists' respective studio albums _[PartyNextDoor 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PartyNextDoor_4 "PartyNextDoor 4")_ (2024) and _[For All the Dogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_All_the_Dogs "For All the Dogs")_ (2023). It marks PartyNextDoor's first collaborative project and Drake's third, after 2015's _[What a Time to Be Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_a_Time_to_Be_Alive "What a Time to Be Alive")_ (with [Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_\(rapper\) "Future (rapper)")) and 2022's _[Her Loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her_Loss "Her Loss")_ (with [21 Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21_Savage "21 Savage")). The album was released among the backdrop of Drake's ongoing legal dispute with [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") (UMG) and was his first full-length release following [his feud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake–Kendrick_Lamar_feud "Drake–Kendrick Lamar feud") with [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar"). _Some Sexy Songs 4 U_ was supported by four singles, including "[Nokia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nokia_\(song\) "Nokia (song)")" and "[Die Trying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Trying_\(PartyNextDoor,_Drake,_and_Yebba_song\) "Die Trying (PartyNextDoor, Drake, and Yebba song)")". The pair embarked on the [Some Special Shows 4 U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Some_Special_Shows_4_U "Some Special Shows 4 U") tour in support of the album.

_Some Sexy Songs 4 U_ opened with first-week sales of 246,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_units "Album-equivalent units") in the United States and debuted at number one on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), marking PartyNextDoor's first chart-topper and Drake's fourteenth, tying him with [Jay-Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay-Z "Jay-Z") and [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") for the most number-one albums on the chart by solo artists. It also topped the [albums chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Canadian_Albums "Billboard Canadian Albums") in the artists' native of Canada. Internationally, it peaked in the top ten in Australia, Belgium, the Netherlands, Ireland, Lithuania, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. Upon its release, the album received mixed reviews from critics, who praised its production and intimate nature, but criticized the runtime and lyricism.

The album follows the pair's numerous collaborations since PartyNextDoor was signed to Drake's record label, [OVO Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OVO_Sound "OVO Sound"), back in 2013, with the first of these being Drake's guest appearance on "Over Here" from PartyNextDoor's [eponymous mixtape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PartyNextDoor_\(mixtape\) "PartyNextDoor (mixtape)") (2013).[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) Alongside their collaborations, they have contributed to each other's individual songs as a writer or producer.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) PartyNextDoor supported the release of his album _[PartyNextDoor 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PartyNextDoor_4 "PartyNextDoor 4")_ (2024) through a twenty-four-stop Canada and U.S. live tour.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) On August 2, 2024, at the tour's stop at the [Budweiser Stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budweiser_Stage "Budweiser Stage") in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto")—the artists' hometown—Drake performed as a surprise guest, with his set foregoing any of the hip-hop tracks in his discography.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) He then announced the collaborative album, saying, "On behalf of me and Party, we've been working on something for y'all. So, you get the summer over with, you do what you need to do. I know all you girls are outside. When it gets a little chilly, PartyNextDoor and Drake album will be waiting right there for you".[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

Just two days later, the OVO [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") page seemingly hinted at the album by posting backstage pictures of Drake and PartyNextDoor that was taken after the concert.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) During an interview on August 5, PartyNextDoor revealed that his favorite collaboration with Drake "\[are\] the \[ones\] we \[are\] doing right now. All 15 of them", seemingly revealing that the pair were working on 15 songs for the album.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) On August 6, Drake released 100 gigabytes of data, including behind-the-scenes clips, tour rehearsals, and studio footage. He also previewed three unreleased tracks (tracks of which what would later be released as the _[100 Gigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100_Gigs "100 Gigs")_) under an Instagram page by the name "plottttwistttttt".[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) On August 7, video clips surfaced of nightclubs in Canada previewing unreleased music from the album.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) On the same day, via the "plottttwistttttt" Instagram account, Drake reposted a tweet, blurring out the words "album rollout" regarding another unheard track.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)

On October 5, Drake attended at [Tyrone Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrone_Edwards "Tyrone Edwards")' Nostalgia Party in Toronto, where he called out his "fake friends" in the music industry and cited PartyNextDoor as a "real" friend. He also hinted at the album's impending release by saying "shoutout to my brother PX, album dropping soon".[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) In an appearance on _The Fry Yiy Show_ on [SiriusXM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SiriusXM "SiriusXM") that same month, OVO engineer, [Noel Cadastre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Cadastre "Noel Cadastre"), stated that the album only required "finishing touches" and called November "a jam-packed month for me \[to finish the album\]". PartyNextDoor then revealed work on the album would continue after the conclusion of the European leg of his Sorry I'm Outside Tour on November 6, saying, "I have one more show on this tour, then the album is getting finished".[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) During a [Kick live stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kick_\(service\) "Kick (service)") with [xQc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XQc "XQc") on November 24, Drake stated the album was almost complete, saying, "\[the\] album is 75 percent done. Shout out to PX, cooking right now," and added that "the album sounds incredible... It's the sound people know and love us for".[\[22\]](#cite_note-22) On December 26, Drake appeared on a Kick live stream with [Adin Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adin_Ross "Adin Ross"), in which he stated that the album is one of the records that he is "most proud of in \[his\] life". He also revealed that the album was supposed to release in November, but was delayed.[\[23\]](#cite_note-:01-23)

_Some Sexy Songs 4 U_'s release follows legal action by Drake against [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") (UMG), the parent company of [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), with whom Drake has a [recording contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_contract "Recording contract"). In November 2024, Drake initiated a legal petition against UMG and [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") in the U.S., alleging they conspired to artificially inflate the number of streams of the [diss track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diss_track "Diss track"), "[Not Like Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not_Like_Us "Not Like Us")" by [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar") on the service during Drake's [feud with Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake–Kendrick_Lamar_feud "Drake–Kendrick Lamar feud") earlier that year by implementing [pay-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payola "Payola"), [malicious bots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_bot#Malicious_bots "Internet bot"), and other tactics.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) Drake withdrew the petition on January 14, 2025, and filed a [lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawsuit "Lawsuit") in U.S. district court a day later, alleging [defamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation "Defamation") against UMG for promoting "Not Like Us".[\[25\]](#cite_note-Variety-25) This legal dispute caused confusion regarding which label or company would act as the distributor for _Some Sexy Songs 4 U_.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-Skit-27) It was eventually released through OVO, Santa Anna, and Republic, each of which are the artists' labels, while it was distributed through Santa Anna (owned by [Sony Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music "Sony Music")), but licensed to Republic.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28)

On February 3, 2025, the album's title was revealed and its release date of February 14 was announced.[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) The announcement included a snippet of "Deeper".[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)[\[2\]](#cite_note-$$$-2) On February 9, Drake shared a snippet of the song "Crying in Chanel".[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) A day later, Drake shared a promotional skit for the album starring the Canadian comedic duo Jermaine and Trevaunn Richards, which depicted Trevaunn practicing a romantic speech with his brother for his girlfriend but being unable or unwilling to tell her that he loves her. According to Jon Powell of [Revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolt_TV "Revolt TV"), this exemplifies the "playful, self-aware marketing that helped Drake maintain his cultural dominance for well over a decade".[\[27\]](#cite_note-Skit-27) Drake previously collaborated with the Richards by making a cameo appearance in the duo's "T-Dot Goon Scrap DVD 2" comedy sketch in May 2017.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32)

The following day, Drake shared the album's official cover art via Instagram,[\[33\]](#cite_note-Artwork-33) which depicted Drake (left) and PartyNextDoor (right) standing together during a snowstorm in front of [Absolute World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_World "Absolute World") in [Mississauga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississauga "Mississauga"), Ontario, wearing oversized fur coats.[\[33\]](#cite_note-Artwork-33)[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) On February 12, Drake shared a snippet of the track "[Somebody Loves Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somebody_Loves_Me_\(PartyNextDoor_and_Drake_song\) "Somebody Loves Me (PartyNextDoor and Drake song)")" on "@plottttwistttttt".[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) He also shared a photo of the title page of December 2024-draft of a [screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenplay "Screenplay") called "$$$ 4 U" (the acronym for the album title): it listed Drake and PartyNextDoor as its writers and that it was based on an unreleased novel of the same name by Drake's father, Dennis Graham.[\[36\]](#cite_note-36) A day later, Drake revealed the album's 21-song tracklist via Instagram and confirmed its runtime to be 74 minutes.[\[37\]](#cite_note-37)

In October 2025, PartyNextDoor released _$$$_, a short film inspired by the album.[\[38\]](#cite_note-38)

On February 13, 2025, some social media users and [Freddie Gibbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Gibbs "Freddie Gibbs") accused Drake and PartyNextDoor of plagiarizing use of the dollar symbol in the album's title and bunnies in its promotional material from Gibbs' album _[Soul Sold Separately](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Sold_Separately "Soul Sold Separately")_ (2022).[\[39\]](#cite_note-39)[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](#cite_note-41) Canadian rapper John River accused Drake and PartyNextDoor of plagiarizing the pose in front of Absolute World in the album's artwork from his music video to his 2021 single "Hope City II": he claimed PartyNextDoor and "another OVO artist" contacted him "obsessing" over his video and "thought process", but threatened to [blackball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blacklisting "Blacklisting") him after River refused to act as a [ghostwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostwriter "Ghostwriter").[\[42\]](#cite_note-:0-42)[\[43\]](#cite_note-43)

## Music and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Some_Sexy_Songs_4_U&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Music and composition")\]

_Some Sexy Songs 4 U_ contains twenty-one tracks, with a playing time of over 73 minutes.[\[44\]](#cite_note-TNYT-44)[\[45\]](#cite_note-45) Its album release coincides with [Valentine's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine's_Day "Valentine's Day"), marking Drake's third full-length project to be released near that date, after _[So Far Gone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Far_Gone_\(mixtape\) "So Far Gone (mixtape)")_ (2009) and _[If You're Reading This It's Too Late](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_You're_Reading_This_It's_Too_Late "If You're Reading This It's Too Late")_ (2015); according to _[HotNewHipHop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HotNewHipHop "HotNewHipHop")_, Drake's albums released during this time "reflect his shifting perspectives on love, success, and emotional vulnerability", saying, "Few artists have aligned themselves with a holiday like Drake has with Valentine's Day".[\[46\]](#cite_note-46)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Noah_Shebib.jpg/250px-Noah_Shebib.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Noah_Shebib.jpg)

_Some Sexy Songs 4 U_ is Drake's first album to not include longtime collaborator and friend [40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40_\(producer\) "40 (producer)") as a producer.

According to Will Schube and Kia Turner of _[Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_Networks "Complex Networks")_, _Some Sexy Songs 4 U_ primarily mixes elements of [contemporary R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B"), [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), and [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music").[\[47\]](#cite_note-Clash-47)[\[48\]](#cite_note-Complex-48) It also explores [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock"), [acoustic pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"),[\[48\]](#cite_note-Complex-48) and [regional Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Mexican "Regional Mexican") on certain songs.[\[44\]](#cite_note-TNYT-44) The album features production from several different producers, which was handled primarily by Drake's longtime collaborators [Noel Cadastre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Cadastre "Noel Cadastre"), [Gordo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordo_\(DJ\) "Gordo (DJ)"), [Jordan Ullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majid_Jordan "Majid Jordan") and PartyNextDoor himself, alongside PartyNextDoor's frequent collaborators Alex Lustig, Niketaz, and Niko.[\[49\]](#cite_note-49)

According to Joe Coscarelli of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_, the lyrical themes on the album are reminiscent of both Drake and PartyNextDoor's previous works, including Drake's _[Dark Lane Demo Tapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Lane_Demo_Tapes "Dark Lane Demo Tapes")_ (2020) and PartyNextDoor's _[PartyNextDoor 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PartyNextDoor_3 "PartyNextDoor 3")_ (2016).[\[44\]](#cite_note-TNYT-44) On the album, Drake takes several shots at other artists, including [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar") and [Joe Budden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Budden "Joe Budden"), while he makes references to [Charli XCX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charli_XCX "Charli XCX") and her album _[Brat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brat_\(album\) "Brat (album)")_ (2024), [21 Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21_Savage "21 Savage"), and [Tate McRae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_McRae "Tate McRae").[\[50\]](#cite_note-NME-50)

Throughout the record, "Drake's attention remains primarily on the ladies" while PartyNextDoor "opens up about his sexual escapades", according to _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_'s Carl Lamarre and Michael Saponara.[\[51\]](#cite_note-BB_Ranked-51) Drake covers the topics of a [bachelor lifestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor "Bachelor"), settling down, being turned on by his peers, and his previous sexual experiences.[\[51\]](#cite_note-BB_Ranked-51)[\[52\]](#cite_note-Vibe-52) Similarly, PartyNextDoor covers themes of sex, money, [infidelity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infidelity "Infidelity"), and [sexual jealousy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_jealousy "Sexual jealousy").[\[51\]](#cite_note-BB_Ranked-51)[\[52\]](#cite_note-Vibe-52)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Ice_Spice_%28color_corrected%29.png/250px-Ice_Spice_%28color_corrected%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ice_Spice_\(color_corrected\).png)

"Glorious" features uncredited vocal samples from a 2023 interview by [Ice Spice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_Spice "Ice Spice").[\[53\]](#cite_note-53)
